c.The Role of the Trial Judge in the Presentation of Evidence
Judges have significant powers to shape the presentation of evidence at trial. To give one example, it is not unusual for judges to
impose time limits for each side to present its case, a practice authorized under Federal Rule 16(c)(2)(O). A “chess clock” trial encourages
the parties to streamline their case, thereby sharpening the issues and reducing the length (and burden) of the trial—an especially
important consideration with a jury. But time limits might also impair the goals of accuracy and procedural justice in trials. See Nora
Freeman Engstrom, The Trouble with Time Limits, 106 Geo. L.J. 933 (2018).

A judge’s powers with respect to other aspects of trial are less certain. Suppose that an attorney’s presentation of a case appears
inadequate. To what extent should the trial judge take over the trial by interrogating the witness herself and perhaps by calling new
witnesses she believes should be heard? Does it make a difference if the case is before a jury? See Blanck, Calibrating the Scales of
Justice: Studying Judges’ Behavior in Bench Trials, 68 Ind.L.J. 1119 (1993). These questions raise fundamental considerations regarding
the role of the trial judge: Is the court a mere umpire who must stand aloof except when called upon to make decisions or a participant
with the right to supervise the conduct of the trial to help ensure a just result?
There is agreement that judges have some limited power to call and interrogate witnesses, although no consensus as to the extent of
that power. Judges may use this power to draw out important facts or clear up confused testimony. The tenor of the judge’s questioning
may also affect the jury’s perception of the evidence. In particular, any apparent bias on the judge’s part may encourage the jury to view
the facts presented by the witness more or less favorably. See Laughlin, Learning from the Past? Or Destined to Repeat Past Mistakes?:
Lessons from the English Legal System and Its Impact on How We View the Role of Judges and Juries Today, 14 Widener L.Rev. 357
(2009). Do you think a judge ought to be required to intercede when the failure to do so might result in a miscarriage of justice? Does
the judge owe a special responsibility to a pro se litigant? See Carpenter, Active Judging and Access to Justice, 93 Notre Dame L.Rev.
647 (2017).
